newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties may let bureaucrats tackle deficit.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties may let bureaucrats tackle deficit.

text.p: Japanese politicians are bashing bureaucrats ahead of an election this month, but are likely to leave the tricky task of cutting the nation's massive budget deficit to much-maligned financial mandarins.

"The solutions are going to be found by the...Finance Ministry," said Chris Calderwood, chief economist at BZW Securities. "It's going to be cold turkey (on public spending) for a very long time, and the politicians are not addressing it because there is no good news to give."

Politicians this week kicked off their campaigns for an October 20 Lower House election with both ruling and opposition camps clamouring for "administrative reform", a broad concept that encompasses varying prescriptions for smaller government and greater political control over policy.

That politicians of every ilk have made such reform their rallying cry owes much to the tarnished reputation of elite bureaucrats following a string of policy missteps ranging from alleged mishandling of banks' bad loan mess to the health ministry's admitted responsibility for a 1980s scandal over HIV-tainted blood products.

"The bureaucrats in their elitism firmly believe they alone should be in charge of everything," said one newspaper editorial. "The unclear power structure has corrupted the bureaucrats and led to such abuse and negligence as the Ministry of Health and Welfare's AIDS scandal," it said.

While politicians appear united in their public disdain for bureaucrats, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) -- now the biggest partner in the ruling bloc -- and the main opposition Shinshinto have taken sharply different stances on taxes.

The Shinshinto wants to woo voters with a Reaganesque call to boost the economy by slashing income and residential taxes while freezing the consumption tax at its current three percent for the rest of this century, steps many economists warn would result in drastic deterioration of public finances.

The LDP, as well as the new reformist Democratic Party, is defending a planned increase in the consumption tax to five percent from next April as vital to broaden the tax base to cope with the budget deficit and a rapidly ageing population.

Dwindling tax revenues from a prolonged economic slump and hefty stimulative packages have yielded a public debt that now accounts for nearly 90 percent of Japan's output -- the worst budget deficit after Italy among leading industrial nations.

The growth in the deficit has been largely the result of government efforts to spend its way out of the recession and a modest economic recovery, if sustained, should help stem the red ink short-term by boosting tax revenues, economists say.

Longer-term, however, demographic trends which mean that one-quarter of the population will be 65 or older by the year 2020 will inevitably translate into a ballooning structural deficit unless cutbacks are made in government spending on so-called entitlements such as pensions and health care.

Finance bureaucrats have been steadily beating the budget reform drum, even at the risk of irritating U.S. counterparts who want Tokyo to pursue economic policies that will keep its fragile recovery on track.

"The current fiscal deficit is at an unsustainable level and from the perspective of economic stability as well, cannot be left unaddressed," said a report by a study panel of the government's Economic Planning Agency this week.

Politicians are paying lip service to the theme, with the LDP pledging to reconsider how budget ceilings are set, the Shinshinto calling for expenditure reform and the Democrats murmuring about a fiscal reform law.

Few details, however, are available since politicians generally have little stomach for drawing voters' attention to the tough choices that will need to be made both on taxation and spending, economists say.

"Everyone seems to be focusing on the cost of government itself, but they will have to address entitlements at some point," Calderwood said. "The demographic changes are written in stone. That's why it's important not to fiddle while the fiscal situation burns."
